strengths: Rigorous and fairly complete theoretical treatment of the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) for classifier neuromanifolds, grounded in a careful spectral analysis of the low-dimensional 'core space' (statistical simplex), including tight eigenvalue bounds (Theorem 1) and Löwner-order bounds (Lemma 2) with matching error analysis (Lemmas 3-5).

Novel and practically appealing random estimator (Hutchinson's estimate) of the full FIM (not just the diagonal) that requires only a single extra backward pass, reuses forward-pass logits, and can target diagonal, block-diagonal, low-rank, or full structure via different scalarizing functions (h, h^DG, h^LR).

Strong theoretical guarantees: the proposed estimator is proven unbiased with a bounded coefficient of variation (CV ≤ √2), in contrast to the empirical FIM (shown to have unbounded worst-case error under adversarial labels, Lemma 4/Proposition 11) and standard Monte Carlo estimators (shown to have unbounded CV via a heavy-tailed counterexample).

Clear connection between the low-dimensional core geometry and the high-dimensional neuromanifold via the pullback/Gauss-Newton relationship (Eq. 4), which is used systematically to lift core-space bounds to deterministic FIM bounds (Propositions 6-11).

Reasonably thorough related-work positioning relative to natural gradient methods, Kronecker-factored approximations, and prior Hutchinson-trace-based Hessian/FIM estimators, clarifying the paper's specific contribution (full-tensor, architecture-agnostic estimator via AD detach tricks).
Proofs are provided in detail in the appendix, aiding reproducibility of the theoretical claims.
weaknesses: Empirical validation is thin: only qualitative density plots of diagonal FIM entries on DistilBERT for two text classification datasets; there is no quantitative comparison against a brute-force/ground-truth FIM to verify the tightness of the proposed bounds or the predicted variance formulas.

No downstream demonstration of practical utility (e.g., natural gradient optimization, pruning, or generalization studies) despite the paper motivating the work via natural gradient and optimization applications in the introduction and related work.
No wall-clock/memory benchmarking comparing the proposed Hutchinson estimator, eFIM, and MC estimator, despite computational efficiency being a central selling point of the method.

Experiments are run on a single CPU (MacBook Pro M1) with a small model (DistilBERT) and small sample sizes (128 examples, 10 Hutchinson samples); it is unclear how the method scales to larger models or how bound tightness behaves for architectures beyond a simple softmax classification head.

The low-rank estimator's reliance on a separately approximated power-iteration for λ_C and v_C introduces an additional source of error that is not incorporated into the paper's variance/CV guarantees.

The contribution, while technically solid, is fairly narrow in scope (single-task classification FIM geometry) and its broader significance/impact for the wider ML community is not strongly established beyond the information-geometry niche.
The presentation is dense and heavily notation-laden; while proofs are deferred to the appendix, the main text could better emphasize practical takeaways and intuition for a broader audience.
